chunks: How a stepper motor works. The question: How does it work?
A stepper motor works by moving a magnetic field in small jumps and letting the rotor (the spinning part, which carries a magnet) chase it.
Powering one coil makes the rotor line up with it. Powering the next coil moves the target slightly, and the rotor follows.
Repeating the sequence turns the shaft one step at a time.
Imagine a compass needle surrounded by electromagnets. Switch on the one to the north, and the needle swings to point at it.
Switch it off and the one to the east on, and the needle swings 90° to face east. Keep stepping around the ring, and the needle turns around in jumps.
The analogy has a gap: real steppers have many small teeth, so each step is much smaller, such as 1. 8°.
A simplified four-pole PM stepper (real hybrids have many more teeth, same idea). Energising coil A as an N pole attracts the rotor's S end to the top.
Turning A off and energising B moves the equilibrium 90° clockwise; the rotor follows. Energising A' next carries it another 90°. Reversing the sequence reverses the direction.
Phase: one of the fixed coil groups, turned on or off in a sequence. Full step: a move made by switching whole phases on.
Microstepping: sharing the current smoothly between the two phases so the rotor settles between full steps, for smoother motion. Open loop: counting pulses without feedback.
Missed step: the rotor falls behind when the load is too big.
A typical stepper (the common "hybrid" kind) has two phases and 50 teeth on its rotor. The angle from one tooth to the next, the tooth pitch, is 360° / 50 = 7. 2° .
A full cycle of the four-state sequence moves the rotor one tooth pitch, so each of the four steps is 7. 2° / 4 = 1. 8° .
Run the sequence the other way and the motor turns the other way. That is the whole idea: step the field, and the rotor follows.
"A stepper moves by walking a magnetic field in small jumps.
Energise a coil and the rotor, a magnet or toothed iron, aligns with it; switch to the next coil and the equilibrium moves one step, so the rotor follows.
In a 2-phase, 50-tooth motor, four steps make one electrical cycle, 7. 2 degrees, each step 1. 8. Driving the phases as sine and cosine gives microsteps.
It runs open loop by counting pulses, and the driver uses current chopping from a high supply voltage so the coil current can build quickly at speed."
